Mantua
MAN-tyoo-uh
n. (the Lombard city of the Gonzaga, named in 1537 as the first site of the general council later held at Trent, and the diocese of Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga)
From Latin Mantua, an Etruscan town name, traditionally derived from the god Mantus.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mantua lies on the Mincio in a loop of lakes, and was governed by the Gonzaga family from 1328 until 1708. In 1537 Paul the Third summoned a general council to meet at Mantua, and that summons is the reason the city belongs in this dictionary: the Protestant princes refused the venue as being in imperial Italy and under papal control, Duke Federico demanded a garrison at papal expense, and the council was postponed, moved to Vicenza, postponed again, and finally opened at Trent in 1545. The eight years of manoeuvre between Mantua and Trent were decisive, because by 1545 the Protestant churches were organised, confessed and governed, and no longer needed the council they had demanded in 1520. The diocese of Mantua was held from 1521 by Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga, a reform-minded prelate who presided at Trent in its final period and died there in 1563. The dictionary records Mantua as the price of delay: a reform postponed for the convenience of princes became a reform refused.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a council as an ecclesiastical assembly; a summons as a call by authority to appear; delay as a putting off or deferring; a venue as the place where a cause is tried; and reform as a change from worse to better.

expand to see more

COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice, especially an assembly of ecclesiastics.

SUMMONS, n. A call by authority or the command of a superior to appear at a place named, or to attend to some duty.

DELAY, n. A putting off or deferring; procrastination; a lingering; stay; stop.

VENUE, n. In law, a neighborhood or near place; the place where an action is laid or a cause tried.

REFORM, n. A change from worse to better; amendment of life or manners; correction of abuses.

Rev 2:5 — "Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent."

Pro 27:1 — "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth."

Modern Corruption

Gonzaga city named in 1537 as the first site of the general council, whose postponement for eight years ended at Trent in 1545.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the use of procedure to avoid a question, and Mantua is the textbook case. Christendom had asked for a free general council since 1520; a pope summoned one in 1537 to a city of imperial Italy, a duke demanded terms, the Protestants objected to the venue, and eight years went by in negotiation while positions hardened on both sides. Nobody in that process said no to reform. Everyone said not here and not yet. Felix's famous adjournment is the same move in one sentence: “Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee” (Act 24:25).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that repentance has a clock. The Lord's word to a declining church is not a proposal to be scheduled but a command with a term attached, “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), and the writer to the Hebrews fixes the day: “To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts” (Heb 3:15). Solomon forbids the confidence that makes delay feel safe, “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Pro 27:1). A church may be lost by a calendar as surely as by a heresy.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek metanoeo (G3340), to repent; Greek kairos (G2540), a season; Hebrew machar (H4279), to morrow.

expand to see more

Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; “and repent, and do the first works”, Revelation 2:5.

Greek kairos (G2540) — a fixed time, a season, an opportunity; “when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee”, Acts 24:25.

Greek semeron (G4594) — to day; “To day if ye will hear his voice”, Hebrews 3:15.

Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; “harden not your hearts”, Hebrews 3:15.

Hebrew machar (H4279) — to morrow, the coming day; “Boast not thyself of to morrow”, Proverbs 27:1.

Usage

"“when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee” (Act 24:25) — the eight years between Mantua and Trent."

"“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts” (Heb 3:15) — repentance has a clock."

"“Boast not thyself of to morrow” (Pro 27:1) — why a postponed reform becomes a refused one."
